title: The Map of a Commerce Platform: Capabilities and Layers
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/03-commerce-capability-map/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter. It is a contract, not a description: the places where the chapter does not yet do what the spec asks are listed under open_questions.

know: About two dozen capabilities in six layers and the kind of business fact each one owns.
The three ways vendors cover the map: suite, platform plus apps, best-of-breed assembly.
believe: A capability is a job the business needs done, not a product; drawing jobs first makes gaps and overlaps visible.
can_do: Place any system or vendor product on the map and say which capabilities it claims.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the engineer, product manager or analyst who has just joined a merchant and needs to understand what all the software is for, and the consultant or leader who must judge a vendor's proposal.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side.
Roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.
Kestrel & Pine, its people and its 2026 incidents, in outline (meet-kestrel-and-pine), and the names of the failure patterns (where-commerce-platforms-go-wrong).

From journey-of-an-order: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, what a system is, 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, the seven systems in the order walk at Kestrel & Pine and the thirteen in its full landscape, and PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and availability service.
From commerce-business-models: the business models (D2C, B2B, wholesale, marketplace selling), and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group).
does_not_know: The map's own vocabulary: capability, layer, business fact, flow, natural home, copy, derived fact, writer, write audit.
PIM, OMS, POS, ATP (available-to-promise), GTIN, Peppol, BI, GMV.
Suite, hosted SaaS platform, app, best-of-breed, composable, MACH, headless, ERP-centered commerce, specialist group.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a vendor's product description, the reader names the capabilities it covers and one it does not.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A vendor says its product 'unifies orders across channels and routes them to the best location'. Which capabilities on the map is that, and which neighbouring capability is not included?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Order management and sourcing; not warehouse management (or not inventory counting).

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a company that describes its landscape as a list of systems, the reader says why gaps and overlaps cannot be seen in that list and what to draw to see them.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A company lists its software: a shop platform, an ERP and a warehouse system, each with a stock field. Using only this chapter: why can the company not tell from that list whether it has a gap or an overlap, and what should it draw to find out?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Every system looks complete from the inside, so a list of systems hides both. Draw the jobs (capabilities) first and place the systems in them afterwards: an overlap shows as one box with several names (here, stock), a gap as an empty box.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a value that is computed from other facts, the reader says that it is derived, what it is computed from, and why editing the result by hand does harm.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A support agent wants to type a higher 'available' number for a jacket into the shop's admin screen, because the web page shows fewer than the warehouse has. Using only this chapter: what kind of fact is that number, how is it produced, and what goes wrong if it is edited by hand?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A derived fact: available-to-promise, computed from stock on hand minus commitments to unshipped orders minus any buffer. Its owner is the calculation; a hand edit bypasses it and lets the storefront promise what the warehouse cannot deliver.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader names the flows that must be exact in near real time and says what the other flows need instead.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: which movements of facts between systems must be exact almost immediately, and what do the other movements need instead?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Prices, orders and payments. The others tolerate lag as long as a reconciliation compares the copies; finance can run as a daily batch.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a merchant that is not a vendor, the reader states the author's rule for covering the map and the work that stays with the merchant whichever vendor it picks.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant with a web shop, stores, a marketplace channel and its own warehouse asks how it should cover the map with products. Using only this chapter: what is the author's rule, and what work stays with the merchant whichever vendor it chooses?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Cover the center with one product it does not customize, cover operations with products built for operations, and own the joins itself. The joins (the integration between the boxes) stay with the merchant; no vendor covers the whole map.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader new to commerce meets no term in this chapter before it is explained, and every acronym is expanded on first use.

thesis.question: What are all the parts of a commerce platform, what does each do, and how do they usually connect?
thesis.claim: A commerce platform is best mapped as capabilities, the jobs the business needs done, each owning one kind of business fact; systems are placed on that map afterwards, and no vendor covers all of it.
thesis.disputed_by: The habit of describing a platform as a list of products or vendors, which hides both the jobs nobody does and the jobs two systems both claim.
thesis.so_what: Where two systems both believe they own a fact is where money leaks; the map is the tool that finds those places before an incident does.
thesis.how_why: Products bundle and split jobs differently per vendor, so only the jobs are stable enough to compare one landscape with another.

supporting_claims.claim: Drawing the jobs first and placing the systems afterwards shows the gaps and overlaps that a list of systems hides.
The jobs fall into about two dozen capabilities in six layers, and each capability is the natural home of one kind of business fact, recorded or derived, while every other holder keeps a copy.
A small number of flows join the capabilities, each with its own need for freshness and exactness, and the joins are where copies arrive late, get lost or get duplicated.
Vendors cover the map in three ways, none covers all of it, and the joins between what they cover stay with the merchant.
The map stays the same as a merchant grows; what changes is how many boxes need their own system.
Read against the map, a product page, a landscape or an incident shows which boxes are claimed, empty, written by several systems or held by the wrong one, before the business feels it.

role.contribution: Turns the journey and the business models into a stable map of jobs, which the ownership chapter then assigns facts on.

additional_patterns.applies_to: map: layers, then capabilities, then notes on the table, then the derived facts
three-ways and when-it-goes-wrong: parallel options and parallel failures

flow.rationale: The chapter builds the map, then uses it twice. Building: the scene shows the method working once, so the reader wants the terms; the definitions come before the map because the map is drawn in them, and placed after it the table's 'fact' column would have no meaning; the flows follow the boxes because an arrow needs two boxes. First use, vendors: the three ways come only after boxes and flows because coverage is measured in boxes and joins, and reading one product page follows directly because it asks of a single product what the three ways asked of a kind of product; with the stages between them, as published, the two vendor sections were split by a section about the merchant. The vendors come before the merchant's own landscape because that landscape is made of bought products: the stage table and the failures speak of shop platforms, apps and suites, which would be unexplained if the order were reversed. Second use, the merchant's own landscape: the stages come first because they say how many boxes should be filled at all; the four failures follow because one of them (the giant's map) is the stage test broken and the others need the 'home', 'copy' and 'writer' of the map; Kestrel & Pine's landscape comes last because its table shows three of the failures at once and its plan uses the repair the failures section names (a single writer per fact). Told before the failures, as published, the plan applied repairs the reader had not met; and ending the body on the whiteboard returns to the scene the chapter started from.

hook.content: A merchant asks for store pickup. Checkout, the store and the stock system all have to cooperate, and buying a pickup app helps only if the app can get stock reserved and tell store staff what to prepare.

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone who has joined a merchant has heard a request like 'add store pickup' answered with 'there is an app for that'.
bridge.to_topic: The request is a change to several business jobs at once, so the first question is which jobs, and which systems do them today: that is a map of capabilities.

thesis_statement.text: A capability is a job the business needs done, not a product; every capability owns one kind of business fact; draw the map in capabilities first and place systems on it, and no vendor covers all of it.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout, all three bullets; paragraph p01 defines a capability in prose

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and paragraph p03, the last paragraph of the introduction

promises.promise: Start from the whiteboard on which Kestrel & Pine drew its jobs before its systems.
Define the terms, then lay out about two dozen capabilities in six layers with the fact each one owns.
Add the flows that connect the capabilities.
Place vendors on the finished map: the three ways products cover it, and how to read one product page against it.

End with a merchant's own landscape: how many boxes need their own system at each scale stage, the four ways a landscape goes wrong on the map, and Kestrel & Pine's thirteen systems placed box by box.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A request such as store pickup needs several systems to cooperate, so working out what must change starts from the business jobs involved; a capability is one such job, and several systems may contribute to it.

evidence.what: A merchant asks for store pickup: checkout, the store and the stock system must cooperate, and a pickup app helps only if it can get stock reserved and tell store staff what to prepare.
evidence.shows: One ordinary request touches several jobs, so a product bought for it does not settle what must change.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Without a shared view of which capability must change, which system handles it and who depends on its answer, teams buy overlapping tools and leave the handoff between them unowned.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine reached 34 integrations and 41 apps through individually reasonable decisions.
evidence.shows: Overlap and unowned handoffs build up one sensible purchase at a time.

transition_in.carries_over: Starting from the business jobs involved.
transition_in.introduces: Two further requests, the three questions the approach asks, and what happens without a shared view.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each step Eva's jacket passed through in the previous chapter is a capability on the map this chapter draws, and each handoff is a connection that someone must build and own.

transition_in.carries_over: Capabilities, the systems that handle them and the handoffs between them.
transition_in.introduces: The order from journey-of-an-order, whose steps are capabilities and whose handoffs are connections.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter draws the shared view as a map: it starts from Kestrel & Pine's whiteboard, defines the terms, lays out the capabilities in six layers with the fact each owns, adds the flows, places vendors on the finished map (the three ways products cover it, and how to read a product page), and ends with a merchant's own landscape (how many boxes need their own system at each stage, the four ways a landscape goes wrong, and Kestrel & Pine's systems placed box by box).

transition_in.carries_over: The need for a shared view of capabilities and connections, now tied to the order the reader already followed.
transition_in.introduces: The map as the shared view, the order in which the chapter builds and uses it, and the two chapters that take over from it.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: A Whiteboard in February 2027
sections.controlling_idea: Drawing the jobs needed to sell a jacket before placing the thirteen systems showed Kestrel & Pine, within an hour, the gaps and overlaps that five years of buying systems one at a time had hidden.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the method working once, at one company, before any term is defined.

flow.rationale: January's scattered knowledge, February's whiteboard, what it showed within the hour, March's program: told in any other order the findings would come before the method that produced them.

transition_in.carries_over: The claim that a shared view of the jobs must come before the systems.
transition_in.introduces: The morning one company drew that view, and what it showed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In January 2027 Kestrel & Pine had thirteen systems and no shared picture of them: the integrations, the apps and what reached the ERP were each known to a different person.

evidence.what: Ruben Alves tracked the 34 integrations, Milan Petrov knew the 41 apps, Sanne de Wit knew what reached the ERP.
evidence.shows: The knowledge existed and was not joined.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Noor drew the jobs needed to sell a jacket first and placed the thirteen systems into those boxes only afterwards, and starting with the jobs made the gaps visible.

evidence.what: The jobs on the whiteboard: show the jacket, price it, check stock, take the order and payment, pick, ship, accept a return, invoice and count the sale.
evidence.shows: The jobs can be listed without naming a system.

transition_in.carries_over: Thirteen systems and no shared picture.
transition_in.introduces: The whiteboard, drawn jobs first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Within an hour the whiteboard showed four empty boxes (product information and order management, then customer identity and availability, which had no owner either, with the delivery promise unowned in a smaller way) and one box with six writers (warehouse stock), a writer being any system, app or person that can change a fact.

evidence.what: No PIM and no OMS; warehouse stock written by the WMS feed, by hand in the ERP, by hand in the platform and by three apps, with the POS writing store stock separately; the Black Friday Oversell of November 2026 (1,340 units oversold, 1,120 orders canceled or delayed, about €96,000) and the App That Wrote Stock of March 2026 (phantom reservations on 600 variants) both on that box.
evidence.shows: The two incidents the reader already knows sit on a box the whiteboard marks.

transition_in.carries_over: Jobs drawn first, systems placed afterwards.
transition_in.introduces: What became visible: empty boxes, a box with six writers, boxes with no owner.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The whiteboard became the first working document of the Waypoint program approved in March, and the rest of the chapter is that whiteboard, generalized.

transition_in.carries_over: What the whiteboard showed.
transition_in.introduces: What it became, and that the chapter now generalizes it.

sections.heading: What a Capability Is, and Why It Comes Before the Systems
sections.controlling_idea: A capability is a job named without reference to who does it, and because systems overlap while jobs do not, only a map drawn in capabilities shows overlaps and gaps.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the whiteboard's boxes and arrows exact names and says why the jobs are drawn first.

flow.rationale: The reason for drawing capabilities first needs the capability and system definitions; facts and flows are defined last because a fact is what a capability keeps and a flow runs between two capabilities.

transition_in.carries_over: The whiteboard's boxes, drawn before the systems.
transition_in.introduces: Exact terms for what was drawn: capability, system, vendor product, business fact, flow.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A capability is a job the business needs done, named without reference to who does it; a system is software that does one or more such jobs, and a vendor product is a system someone sells, usually claiming several capabilities at once.

The distinction matters because systems and vendor products overlap and capabilities do not: drawn in capabilities, an overlap shows as one box with two names and a gap as an empty box, while drawn in systems both are invisible.

evidence.what: The ERP, the WMS and the shop platform all have a stock field, yet there is one job called 'know what is physically on the shelf'.
evidence.shows: Three systems can claim one job, and each looks complete from the inside.

evidence.what: Figure 1: three systems that each look complete beside a grid of capability boxes where one box has three names and another is empty.
evidence.shows: The same landscape hides its overlap and its gap in one drawing and shows them in the other.

transition_in.carries_over: Capability, system and vendor product as three different things.
transition_in.introduces: Why the map is drawn in capabilities.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A business fact is something the business needs to be true about the world and a flow is the movement of a fact, or a request about it, from one capability to another, so the map is boxes and arrows.

transition_in.carries_over: Capabilities as the boxes of the map.
transition_in.introduces: The two remaining terms: business fact and flow.

sections.heading: The Map: Six Layers
sections.controlling_idea: About two dozen capabilities fall into six layers, and each capability is the natural home of one kind of business fact, recorded or derived, while some capabilities hold copies by design.

advances_thesis.how: Lays out the map itself: the layers, the capabilities and the fact each one is the home for.

flow.rationale: After a paragraph on where the map comes from: layers, then the capabilities in them, then three notes on reading the table (two rows, one column, the entries marked as copies), then the derived facts; the notes cannot come before the table they explain, the notes on home and copy sit next to the derived facts because all three are about where a fact lives, and the derived facts come last because they are the exception to the table's rule that a fact is recorded in its home.

transition_in.carries_over: The vocabulary of boxes, facts and arrows.
transition_in.introduces: The boxes themselves, in six layers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The map is the author's synthesis from the specialist vendors' own product descriptions and several product families' capability inventories; it is a teaching map, not a standard.

A layer is a group of capabilities that share a purpose and a rhythm, and from the shopper inward the six layers are experience, offer, transaction, operations, partners and back office, and foundations.

evidence.what: Figure 2: six layers of a commerce platform and the directions in which they feed each other.
evidence.shows: The six layers just named, in one picture, with what each passes to the next.

transition_in.carries_over: The six-layer map.
transition_in.introduces: What a layer is and what each of the six is for.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For each capability the table gives the job in plain words, the business fact it is the natural home for and the chapter that works it out, and the one-line jobs are enough to place a system.

evidence.what: Twenty-four capabilities in six layers: layer, capability, the job in plain words, the fact it is the natural home for, the chapter that owns it.
evidence.shows: Every part of a commerce platform has one row, one job and one fact, so any system can be placed against it.

transition_in.carries_over: The six layers.
transition_in.introduces: The twenty-four capabilities inside them, one row each.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Business-to-business ordering has two rows of its own in the table, the B2B buyer experience and EDI and e-invoicing, because it is a capability in its own right and not an add-on to the web shop.

evidence.what: Eurostat's 2024 figures put EDI-type sales at 11.07% of EU enterprise turnover against 8.39% for web sales, as commerce-business-models showed.
evidence.shows: Orders between companies' systems are too large a share of commerce to be treated as a feature of the web shop.

transition_in.carries_over: The table of capabilities.
transition_in.introduces: The first of three notes on reading it: why business-to-business ordering has its own rows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The 'natural home' column says which system should hold a fact when two systems both hold it: the home is the one system that should write the fact; how to make that decision stick is the next chapter's subject.

transition_in.carries_over: A note on two of the table's rows.
transition_in.introduces: A note on its 'natural home' column.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Several capabilities (the search index, the service view, the marketplace listing, the data warehouse) hold copies by design, which is safe as long as everyone knows they are copies and they are rebuilt from the home, never edited in place.

evidence.what: Figure 3: the capability map as a poster, twenty-four boxes in six bands, with search, service, marketplaces and analytics dashed as copies.
evidence.shows: The table as one picture, with the copies marked.

transition_in.carries_over: The natural home of a fact and its writer.
transition_in.introduces: The entries marked 'a copy' and the rule that makes a copy safe.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Some capabilities own a calculation, not a record: availability is computed as available-to-promise, stock on hand minus commitments to unshipped orders minus any buffer held back.

transition_in.carries_over: Facts that are recorded in a home and copied elsewhere.
transition_in.introduces: Facts that are computed from other facts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A derived fact needs one owner for its calculation whichever product runs it, because editing the result by hand bypasses the calculation and lets the storefront promise what the warehouse cannot deliver.

evidence.what: The delivery promise combines cut-off times, carrier lead times and location in the same way.
evidence.shows: Availability is not the only derived fact.

evidence.what: Figure 4: on hand minus already promised minus buffer equals what a channel may sell.
evidence.shows: The owner of a derived fact is the computation.

transition_in.carries_over: Availability as a calculation.
transition_in.introduces: Who owns a calculation, and what a hand edit does to it.

sections.heading: How the Pieces Talk: The Typical Flows
sections.controlling_idea: Eight typical flows carry facts between capabilities, each with its own need for freshness and exactness, and the joins they form are where commerce platforms fail.

advances_thesis.how: Adds the arrows to the boxes and says which of them must be exact and fast.

flow.rationale: The opening sentence asserts that the arrows differ in rhythm, the table is the evidence, the two patterns are read from it, and the closing claim about the joins needs all three; stated first, that claim would have nothing under it.

transition_in.carries_over: The boxes of the map.
transition_in.introduces: The arrows between them and what each must guarantee.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The arrows carry a small number of fact types, each with its own rhythm: eight flows almost every merchant above the first stage runs, each with a direction, a freshness need, a consistency need and a consequence when it is slow or down.

evidence.what: Eight flows (product content, prices, stock and availability, orders, payments, shipments and tracking, returns and refunds, finance) with from and to, freshness needed, consistency, what happens if slow and if down.
evidence.shows: The requirements differ per flow, so the flows cannot all be built the same way.
evidence.source: The author's judgement from industry practice

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two patterns stand out in the table: only prices, orders and payments need exactness in near real time while everything else tolerates lag if a reconciliation stands behind it, and finance works in periods, not seconds.

evidence.what: Figure 5: product, price and availability flow outward to the channels; orders flow inward and down to the warehouse; stock, shipments and returns flow back; finance receives a daily batch.
evidence.shows: The directions of the flows in one picture.

transition_in.carries_over: The eight flows and their requirements.
transition_in.introduces: The two patterns in them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every arrow is a place where one system's fact becomes another system's copy, and a copy can be late, lost or duplicated, which is why the joins, not the boxes, are where commerce platforms fail.

transition_in.carries_over: The flows and their different requirements.
transition_in.introduces: The joins as the place where failures happen.

sections.heading: Three Ways to Cover the Map
sections.controlling_idea: No vendor sells the whole map: a suite, a platform plus apps and a best-of-breed assembly each cover part of it, and each leaves joins to the merchant.

advances_thesis.how: Places vendors' products on the map and shows what each way of buying leaves uncovered.

flow.rationale: The three ways in parallel, from most covered by one vendor to least, then the two variants, then the comparison of the three ways and the specialist group on one table, then the rule; the rule comes last because it is read off the comparison, and the comparison needs its four options described first.

transition_in.carries_over: The whole map, boxes and arrows.
transition_in.introduces: How products that can be bought cover it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: No merchant builds the whole map and no vendor sells all of it; in practice it is covered in one of three ways, often mixed.

A suite supplies most of the experience, offer and transaction layers in one vendor's data model, so the joins inside the covered boxes are the vendor's problem, while the warehouse, the carriers, the PSP, the marketplaces, the EDI partners and the ERP stay outside.

evidence.what: Salesforce described its Agentforce Commerce release of 6 July 2026 as one platform across B2C, B2B, point of sale and order management.
evidence.shows: A suite's own claim is many boxes in one platform.

evidence.what: Adobe's October 2026 information center lists three ways to run Adobe Commerce and a separate SaaS, Commerce Optimizer, that can work alongside a third-party commerce backend.
evidence.shows: Even a suite vendor sells parts that sit beside someone else's product.

transition_in.carries_over: Three ways to cover the map.
transition_in.introduces: The first: a suite.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A platform plus apps covers the center of the map (storefront to basic order handling) cheaply and well and rents the rest from many small vendors, each writing into the merchant's data, and leaves the operations and partner layers for the merchant to assemble.

evidence.what: Shopify's pricing page in November 2026 lists plans from €28 to a Plus tier 'from €2,100' a month, with lower card rates on higher tiers.
evidence.shows: The center is cheap to start, and the platform also earns from payments.

evidence.what: Lightspeed's fiscal 2026 transaction-based revenue was $815.1 million against subscription revenue of $370.7 million.
evidence.shows: A platform vendor earns more from payments than from subscriptions.

evidence.what: Shopify completed the sale of most of Shopify Logistics to Flexport on 6 June 2023.
evidence.shows: Hosted platforms retreat from the operations layer.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's 41 apps, three of them writing stock.
evidence.shows: Apps are many small vendors writing into the merchant's data.

transition_in.carries_over: One vendor covering many boxes.
transition_in.introduces: A platform that covers the center and rents the edges as apps.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Best-of-breed, or composable, buys one product per box, each best in its class and replaceable, and its cost is the joins.

evidence.what: The MACH Alliance was founded in June 2020 by commercetools, Contentstack, EPAM and Valtech.
evidence.shows: The assembly is a named alternative to the suite.

evidence.what: Manhattan: an OMS is a platform 'designed to track and manage the lifecycle of an order from start to finish'; Akeneo: a PIM is a system 'to centralize, manage, enrich, and distribute product information for commerce'.
evidence.shows: The specialist boxes are real product categories with their own definitions.
evidence.source: Manhattan Associates and Akeneo, n.d., accessed November 2026

evidence.what: The Alliance's February 2026 survey of 600 enterprise technology leaders found 37% naming integration complexity as a primary concern.
evidence.shows: The cost of the joins is admitted by the assembly's own advocates.

evidence.what: Figure 6: the same grid covered by one suite block, by a platform block with app tiles, and by one product per box joined by many lines.
evidence.shows: The three ways differ in who covers the boxes and where the joins fall.

transition_in.carries_over: A platform that covers the center.
transition_in.introduces: One product per box, joined by APIs and an integration platform.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two variants are worth naming: ERP-centered commerce, which makes the ERP the center and the storefront a front end, and a specialist group, which pre-integrates several best-of-breed products under one owner.

evidence.what: Microsoft's documentation of 22 September 2026 says its Business Central Shopify Connector 'is preinstalled for all new sign-ups and trials'.
evidence.shows: ERP plus hosted storefront is a mainstream small-merchant shape.

evidence.what: Katapull, a Dutch group: five companies joined forces on 31 March 2025; on 7 October 2026 a WMS vendor became its eighth label.
evidence.shows: Six operational and partner boxes can come from one group, with the storefront still bought elsewhere.
evidence.source: Katapull public pages; Dutch IT Channel, 2025

transition_in.carries_over: The three main ways.
transition_in.introduces: Two variants of them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Set side by side, the three ways and the specialist group differ in which boxes one vendor covers, where the joins live, who defines 'order' and 'product', the shape of the cost, the time to a first sale, whom each fits and where each limits; ERP-centered commerce has no column because it combines a hosted storefront with an ERP and is not a separate way of buying.

evidence.what: Trade-offs of suite, platform plus apps, best-of-breed and specialist group: boxes covered by one vendor, where the joins live, who defines 'order' and 'product', cost shape, time to first sale, fits, limits.
evidence.shows: Every column has joins that fall to the merchant; the options differ in where.

transition_in.carries_over: The three ways and the two variants, described one by one.
transition_in.introduces: The same options compared on the same seven rows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's rule for a merchant that is not a vendor is to cover the center with one product it does not customize, cover operations with products built for operations, and own the joins itself.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's Waypoint decision W4: stay on the SaaS shop platform and surround it with an OMS, a PIM and an availability service.
evidence.shows: The rule applied to one merchant.

transition_in.carries_over: The trade-offs, where every column leaves joins to the merchant.
transition_in.introduces: The author's rule, and Kestrel & Pine's decision as that rule applied.

sections.heading: Reading a Vendor's Product Page Against the Map
sections.controlling_idea: The map turns a vendor's feature list into three questions: which boxes the product claims, which facts it owns or copies, and what unit is behind its numbers.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the reader the procedure for placing a vendor product on the map.

transition_in.carries_over: No vendor covers the whole map, so every product is a claim on some of its boxes.
transition_in.introduces: A procedure for reading one product's page: which boxes, which facts, which unit.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A product page lists features, and the map turns the list into three questions: which boxes the product claims, which fact it owns and which it copies, and what unit is behind its numbers.

evidence.what: A channel-integration product that claims 'order management' usually imports marketplace orders and pushes status back; a platform that claims 'inventory' usually holds a stock number per location.
evidence.shows: A claimed box is often a flow or a copy.

evidence.what: Fluent Commerce, an OMS vendor: 'your ERP stays the system of record'.
evidence.shows: A vendor can state which fact its product does not own.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: The map does not change with scale; what changes is how many boxes have their own system, and a box deserves one when its capability has more than one producer and more than one consumer and its present holder cannot carry the workflow.

advances_thesis.how: Says when a box needs its own system, so the map is not read as a shopping list.

transition_in.introduces: The merchant's own landscape, and the first thing to ask of it: how many boxes should have their own system at its stage.

evidence.what: Four stages: boxes with their own system, typical shape, warning sign that the shape is ending.
evidence.shows: Each stage fills more boxes and has a sign that it is ending.
evidence.source: The author's judgement; stages from commerce-business-models

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The producer-and-consumer test: a box should get a dedicated system when its capability has more than one producer and more than one consumer and the system that holds it today cannot carry the workflow.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine is at stage 3 with four boxes still empty.
evidence.shows: The company is past the point where the test says to fill them.

evidence.shows: The test gives different answers at different stages for the same box.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: A landscape goes wrong on the map in four ways (an overlap, a gap, a box held by a system bought for another box, and a map copied from a giant), and each is visible on the map before it shows in the business.

advances_thesis.how: Generalizes Kestrel & Pine's marks into four failures a reader can look for, each with how to detect it.

flow.rationale: Four parallel failures: the two about ownership first (too many owners, none), then the two about fit (a system in the wrong box, a map for the wrong size).

transition_in.carries_over: How many boxes a landscape should fill at its stage.
transition_in.introduces: The four ways a landscape gets the filling wrong, each with how it is detected on the map.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The map fails in four ways, and each shows up on the map before it shows up in the business.

evidence.what: Figure 9: four small maps labeled Overlap, Gap, Wrong box and Giant's map.
evidence.shows: The four failures as marks on the map.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An overlap is two systems owning one fact; it is found by a write audit that lists every system, app, script and person that can change the fact, and repaired by naming a single writer and re-publishing the fact from it.

evidence.what: The App That Wrote Stock: a pre-order app adjusted inventory in the platform while the WMS feed also wrote it; 600 variants carried phantom reservations for two weeks. The first weekly reconciliation in May 2027 found 2.3% of active variants with a different quantity between the WMS and the platform (illustrative).
evidence.shows: Two writers of one recorded fact produce differences that only a comparison finds.

transition_in.carries_over: Four failures.
transition_in.introduces: The first: an overlap.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A gap is a fact nobody owns; it fills itself with spreadsheets and copies that start acting as records, shows as the empty box, and is repaired by naming a home before buying a system for it.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's product content lived in four places and its order status in four.
evidence.shows: With no box named, every holder acts as the record.

transition_in.carries_over: A fact with two owners.
transition_in.introduces: A fact with none.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A box held by a system that was bought for a different box works at the stage it was bought in and becomes the bottleneck later; it is found by comparing the box the system was bought for with the boxes it now holds, and repaired by giving the box to a system built for it.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's ERP holds purchasing, the ledger, the item master, manual wholesale orders and the stock master: five jobs, two of them badly.
evidence.shows: A system can cover boxes it was never bought for.

transition_in.carries_over: Facts with too many owners or none.
transition_in.introduces: A fact owned by a system bought for something else.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A map copied from a far larger company gives a stage-2 merchant a system per box and a platform team to run them; the boxes are the same, the number of systems that should fill them is not, and a box that fails the producer-and-consumer test stays inside the shop platform.

evidence.what: A merchant at stage 2 that draws a stage-4 map has bought the Giant's Boots; below the producer-and-consumer test the box stays inside the platform.
evidence.shows: The stage test, not the size of the map, decides how many systems.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the stage test as a limit on filling boxes.

transition_in.carries_over: Boxes held badly.
transition_in.introduces: Boxes filled that did not need filling.

sections.heading: In Practice: Kestrel & Pine's Systems on the Map
sections.controlling_idea: Placed on the map, Kestrel & Pine's thirteen systems leave four boxes empty and several with more than one writer, and the Waypoint decisions are a plan to fill the first and thin the second.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the map to one landscape and shows every 2026 incident on an empty or over-written box.

transition_in.carries_over: The four failures and how each shows on the map.
transition_in.introduces: One whole landscape, Kestrel & Pine's thirteen systems placed box by box, where the first three failures are all found.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Noor's February whiteboard as a table, reduced to the boxes that were not simply covered, shows the four empty boxes, the boxes with several writers and the systems doing jobs they were not bought for, each with what it cost.

evidence.what: Thirteen rows: capability, system in January 2027, status on the map; product information, order management, availability and identity are empty; pricing has three writers (the Price Drift, €179 for nine days, about €8,200 lost); refunds issued by hand in the PSP console (the Double Refund, €19,400); the ERP does five jobs; 62% of wholesale orders through the portal and 38% keyed by hand; 34 integrations.
evidence.shows: Each incident the reader knows sits on an empty box or a box with several writers.

evidence.what: Figure 10: Kestrel & Pine's thirteen systems fill most of the map, but four boxes have no system.
evidence.shows: The table as one picture.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Waypoint decisions read as a plan to fill the empty boxes and thin the overlaps: a PIM, an OMS with an availability service as one of its modules, the WMS as the single writer of physical stock, and integration standards for the arrows, with identity still open.

evidence.what: W3 (PIM, Q3 2027), W1 and W2 (OMS with an availability service, Q4 2027; the WMS as single writer of physical stock), W5 (integration standards).
evidence.shows: Each decision answers one mark on the map.

transition_in.introduces: The decisions that answer them.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The boxes, the arrows and the vendors' coverage are one argument made three times: a fact has one natural home, every other holder is a copy fed by a flow, and a product is a claim on some boxes that leaves the flows between them to the merchant. So three marks on the map (an empty box, a box with more than one writer, a box whose fact is derived) say both where a landscape will fail and what no purchase will fix.
conclusion.so_what: A reader who draws the jobs first finds the places where two systems both believe they own a fact, or none does, before an incident finds them, and reads a vendor's page for what it leaves to the merchant.

callback.to: The store-pickup request of the opening, where a pickup app helps only if it can get stock reserved and tell store staff what to prepare.
callback.how: The reader can now say why in the chapter's terms: pickup is several boxes (cart and checkout, inventory and availability, store operations) and the flows between them, and an app is a claim on one box at most.

takeaway.content: Draw the map in capabilities before systems, mark the empty boxes, the boxes with more than one writer and the boxes whose fact is derived, and take the nine questions to a design review, a vendor demo or the first week in a new company.
